title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hookLine: in the ruins, the mercies of the Lord are not consumed

cards: Here's a strange fact about grief: someone once wrote it out in alphabetical order. The Book of Lamentations is five poems about Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it.
The walls are down, the Temple is ash, children beg for bread in the streets.

And four of the five poems are acrostics: each verse, or each set of verses, starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Maybe it was a way to hold sorrow that has no shape.
And right in the middle of the middle poem, something turns.

teach.h: I AM THE ONE WHO HAS SEEN AFFLICTION.
teach.b: Chapter three is the longest poem, sixty-six verses, three for each letter. A man says, in effect: I am the one who has seen affliction.
He's been walled in, weighed down with chains, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken on gravel. His hope, he says, has perished.
Then at verse twenty-one: this I call back to mind, and so I have hope.
And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed. They are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness."
Commiserations is an old word for compassion.
In Hebrew it's rachamim, which shares its root with the word for womb, and some readers hear a mother's love in it. Notice what the poet doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is fine.
The ruins are still there when he looks up. He says the mercies are not used up.
Like manna in the desert, they don't keep overnight; they come new each morning, enough for the day. Tradition gives the book to Jeremiah, though the poems name no author.
In the older Holy Week services called Tenebrae, Catholics sang Lamentations in the dark, candles going out one by one. Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple.
Both keep this book for the worst days, because it doesn't pretend. It just finds, in the middle of the alphabet, one thing that hasn't run out.

how: Catholics have sung passages of Lamentations at Tenebrae during Holy Week, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering or Morning Prayer, thanking God before anything else.

o: compassion, from the same root as womb
a lament sung over a ruined city

games.q: in the ruins — tap the pairs.
p: each verse starts with the next letter
the Jewish day of mourning for the Temple

s: Lamentations says the city has been rebuilt
the ruins are still there. the poet says the mercies are not used up, not that the loss is over.
most of Lamentations is written as an alphabet acrostic
four of its five poems follow the Hebrew alphabet; chapter three gives three verses to each letter.
the book names Jeremiah as its author
tradition gives it to Jeremiah; the poems themselves name no author.

games.q: you're the poet. your city is ash and your hope, you say, has perished. what do you write next?
o: that everything is fine after all.
that the mercies of the Lord are not used up; they're new every morning.
games.why: "they are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." the ruins don't go away; the mercies come anyway.

practice: Look back over the last day for one mercy that came anyway, in the middle of everything else: a text from someone, hot water, a person who was kind on a bad day.
Hold it for a moment, and let tomorrow's first words, before the phone, be thank you for one thing. If you pray, it can be to God, with this line from Lamentations.

wordCard.voice: rachamim. Hebrew for compassion, kin to the word for womb: the Lord's mercies that aren't used up, but come fresh each morning. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: new (plural), from Lamentations 3:23, new every morning.

carryVoice: Your line: his mercies are new. Not used up, even in the ruins. Until tomorrow.
